analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 0.1% tax on purchases of stocks, bonds, and derivatives.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee; it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a 0.1% excise tax on every purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives traded on U.S. exchanges or involving U.S. parties [S2][S3]. It exempts new issues of securities and very short-term debt like Treasury bills, and it taxes deals routed through foreign subsidiaries of U.S. firms so companies cannot dodge it by trading abroad [S2][S3]. The revenue would go to the federal treasury, making high-frequency trading — a profit engine concentrated in a few large firms — a new source of public funds [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, because the tax falls on high-volume securities trading done mostly by hedge funds, high-frequency traders, and other large institutions rather than on wages or purchases; the revenue would fund the government without raising income or payroll taxes. A 0.1% rate is small on a single household trade but adds up sharply for firms that buy and sell millions of times a day [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, especially middle- and lower-income households

how_it_helps.text: Taxes each purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives at 0.1%, a rate designed to collect the most from high-volume institutional traders rather than from wages or everyday purchases
Exempts initial issues of securities and short-term debt with maturities of 100 days or less, sparing most new corporate borrowing and ordinary Treasury bill financing
Reaches trades by controlled foreign corporations — U.S.-owned companies booked abroad — and requires their U.S. shareholders to pay the tax, blocking the easiest route to moving trades offshore
Directs the Treasury Secretary to write rules with the SEC and CFTC to prevent avoidance, including the use of non-U.S. middlemen in transactions

analysis.who_pays: Securities trading firms — hedge funds, high-frequency traders, market makers, and asset managers — whose profit margins depend on very high trading volume at very low per-trade cost. Some of the cost would also reach ordinary investors: academic studies of transaction taxes find a meaningful share is passed through to holders of mutual funds and 401(k) accounts through higher trading costs and slightly lower returns.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-volume trading firms; partly retirement savers

drawbacks.text: A trading tax is not perfectly targeted: economists have estimated that a meaningful portion of a transaction tax's cost would be borne by ordinary savers through the mutual funds and 401(k) portfolios that trade stocks, not just by Wall Street firms

The bill does not dedicate its revenue to any specific purpose; it simply adds to general federal revenue, so the benefit to any particular group of working people depends entirely on what Congress later spends it on

Traders have strong incentives to shift activity to untaxed foreign venues or outside the definitions of the bill, which could erode revenue and require ongoing regulatory patching — the text itself directs Treasury to write rules 'to prevent avoidance'
Critics of transaction taxes argue they reduce market liquidity, raising trading costs for everyone including retirement savers

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is a progressive revenue source: 0.1% per trade costs a household making a few trades a year almost nothing, while extracting billions from high-frequency and institutional trading. The main honest cost is leakage to ordinary investors through the funds they own and the risk that trades migrate offshore faster than the anti-avoidance rules can follow. On balance the design is aimed at concentrated trading profits, but it is not as cleanly targeted as its supporters claim.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Wall Street Tax Act on March 5, 2019, with 16 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day
Thirty House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total; no Republicans signed on
The full action history shows only two actions — introduction and referral to Ways and Means — with no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing all unenacted bills including this one

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The securities trading industry — hedge funds, high-frequency trading firms, market makers, and asset managers — never faced the 0.1% tax, because the Ways and Means Committee took no action and the bill died without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-volume trading firms and hedge funds

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Wall Street Tax Act of 2019 and recruited cosponsors

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after referral; the bill received no action for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Securities and investment industry
against.role: Trading firms, asset managers, and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed financial transaction taxes in Congress during this period, arguing they would hurt markets and retirement savers

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Democrats, none of the House's 197 Republicans signed on, and the bill died in committee controlled by the Democratic majority.

industries.industry: Securities trading firms (hedge funds, high-frequency traders, market makers)
industries.note: The bill puts a 0.1% tax on every purchase they make; firms that profit from millions of trades a day at razor-thin margins would bear the heaviest burden. Their gain in killing the bill is revenue ordinary taxpayers did not have to replace elsewhere.

industries.industry: Asset managers and mutual funds (including retirement funds)
industries.note: Funds buying and selling securities would pay the tax, and a share of the cost would reach ordinary savers through fund expenses. However, a tax that penalizes rapid churn lightly touches long-term buy-and-hold investors.

The bill makes U.S. exchanges responsible for collecting the tax on trades subject to their rules, adding a compliance role; if trading shifts to foreign venues to avoid the tax, U.S. exchanges also lose volume.
